title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
hook: three weeks, three tracks, one last day on each: the kitchen, the song and the question
carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
tomorrow: guided visits: what a Sikh means by seva

segments.voice: Yesterday, one more day on your track: karma, bhakti or jnana. Serving, singing or asking. Which one did you carry into the day? Today the three tracks end. Day three hundred twenty-two.

Picture three people on the same evening. One is at a community kitchen, sleeves rolled up, ladling dal for strangers, and she has stopped counting the hours a long time ago. One is on a floor cushion with an old book of love songs, reading the same verse twice because it's too beautiful to leave. One is sitting in a quiet room, eyes closed, asking a question so simple it's almost rude: who is it that's sitting here? Three weeks ago you picked one of these people to walk beside. Today is the last day of that walk, and all three get to speak.
screen: `THE KITCHEN.` → `THE SONG.` → `THE QUESTION.` → `THE LAST DAY OF THE TRACK.`

segments.voice: The kitchen first. The karma track ended in seva as a life: service with no bill attached. Not a weekend of volunteering, but a way of holding every job, the paid ones and the unpaid ones, as an offering. The Gita's third chapter said it; Vivekananda said it in New York; people on this track are still saying it with a ladle in their hand. Then the song. The bhakti track ended in the Gita Govinda, a Sanskrit poem by the twelfth-century poet Jayadeva, about Radha and Krishna: longing, a quarrel, a reunion in a forest by the river. Tradition says it has been sung at the Jagannath temple in Puri for centuries, and dancers across India still perform it. Devotees hear the love story as the soul's longing for God. Then the question. The jnana track ended with Ramana Maharshi, who as a teenager in Tamil Nadu lay down and asked what dies when the body dies. He spent the rest of his life at the hill of Arunachala, and his teaching fits in three words: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a job, he said, in effect. Follow the thought I back to where it rises, and rest there. Three very different evenings. And here's something the Gita says in its fifth chapter, about the way of knowledge and the way of action: it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of them as separate. Many teachers hear that as true of all three ways. Hindus have argued for centuries about how the paths fit together, and they still do. This path doesn't settle that argument. It just notices that all three begin with the same small word. Karma. Action, from a root that means to do. The ladle is a doing. The song is a doing. Even the question is a doing.
screen: `KARMA: SEVA AS A LIFE.` · `BHAKTI: THE GITA GOVINDA.` · `JNANA: RAMANA'S WHO AM I?` · `ALL THREE BEGIN WITH A DOING.` · then, large: `KARMA.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the track you walked come back to you. If it was the kitchen, bring to mind one piece of work you did this month for someone else. If it was the song, let one line or one name you love be there, quietly. If it was the question, let the word I rise and gently look for where it comes from. If you didn't pick a track at all, just watch the breath: it's a doing too. No grade, no finish line. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, from the Sanskrit root kri, to do. The first name on three tracks, and the ground under all of them: serving, singing and asking are all things a person does.

Your line: karma, seva as a life; bhakti, the Gita Govinda; jnana, Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry. Today, do one thing from your track on purpose: serve once, sing once, or ask once. Day three hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Hindus often speak of three great paths: karma (selfless action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge). Many people lean toward one, and many teachers say the paths meet; schools differ on how.

match.prompt: each track and where it ended — tap the pairs.
pairs: from a root meaning to do

myth: this path ranks the three tracks, with knowledge as the advanced one
the tracks are electives, never ranked. Hindu teachers have long argued about how they fit; this path doesn't settle it.
the Gita Govinda is a love poem about Radha and Krishna
Jayadeva's twelfth-century Sanskrit poem; devotees hear the love story as the soul's longing for God.
Ramana Maharshi taught by asking people to answer 'who am I?' with their name
the opposite: not a name or a job. follow the thought 'I' back to its source and rest there.

fork.setup: someone asks you which of the three paths is the real one. what does the Gita's fifth chapter say?
options: knowledge is the real one; the others are warm-ups.
only the childish treat the ways as rivals.
action is the real one; the rest is talk.
fork.reveal: the Gita (5.4) says it's the childish, not the wise, who speak of knowledge and action as separate; many teachers extend that to all three. Hindus still debate how the paths fit together.

original.note: Sanskrit karma, action, from the root kṛ, to do.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma means what comes back around to you.
what it means: action itself, from a root meaning to do; the results came to share the name.
what a scholar hears: karma, jnana and bhakti as three named yogas owe much to the Gita's structure, and modern teachers like Vivekananda made the threefold scheme familiar.

notes: Last day of the lineage track (302–322) and of week 46. One script serves listeners on all three tracks; each track gets its last beat. Days 302–321 were not written by this writer, so the recap names the track endings from the outline only.

Gita 5.4: paraphrased as 'the childish, not the wise' speak of sankhya and yoga as different. The verse is about sankhya (knowledge/renunciation) and yoga (action); applying it to all three paths is an interpretation. Please confirm the framing.
Claim that the Gita Govinda has been sung at the Jagannath temple, Puri, for centuries is marked 'tradition says'; please confirm.
Ramana Maharshi: death experience at about 16 (1896) in Madurai, then Tiruvannamalai/Arunachala until 1950. The self-inquiry summary is paraphrased from Nan Yar; check.
The index word 'karma' and the carry (the whole track line) are kept exactly; the carry is long for a spoken line.
